label: Postgres
description: Runs a query against a Postgres database, or inserts a row.

params.name: query
params.label: Query
params.placeholder: SELECT id, region, total FROM orders WHERE total > 1000

params.name: columns
params.label: Columns
params.hint: The column name and the value to write, one row per item.

docs.summary: Runs a SQL query against a database, or inserts a row.
docs.mode: `executeQuery` runs once and returns one item per row. `insert` runs once per item.
docs.when: Use it when the data lives in your own database rather than behind an API — much of the useful data in a real company does.

params.name: operation
params.text: `executeQuery` runs the SQL you write. `insert` writes one row per item, without you writing SQL.

params.name: query
params.text: The SQL. Expressions are allowed, so a query can be built from the incoming item.

params.name: table
params.text: For `insert`: the table to write to.

params.name: columns
params.text: For `insert`: the column name and the value, one row per item.

examples.label: One item per returned row
examples.code: SELECT id, region, total FROM orders WHERE total > 1000

examples.label: Insert one row per item
examples.code:
operation: insert
table:     flagged_orders
columns:   order_id = ={{ $json.id }}
           reason   = high value

gotchas: A query returning no rows gives you 0 items, which makes every node after it report "no items". That is the query, not the workflow.
`insert` runs once per item, so it writes as many rows as it received items.

Inside this simulation every service — including the database — sits behind the same fixture layer, so the run log shows the query as a call to a mock host. One default-deny transport for everything is worth more here than imitating the Postgres wire protocol.
